prompt.context: Our client, FC Limited (Fine China Limited), manufactures sets of fine china (plates, tea cups, etc.). They only sell the china in sets (never as individual pieces) at $1,500 per set. Excess or lack of demand has never been a problem for FC, and they sell 10,000 sets per year. The company was started 50 years ago and has been successful and profitable throughout its history. However, in the last 7 years a key competitor recently entered the industry. FC recently learned that the competitor has at least 50% higher margins and would like to match or exceed its results.
prompt.question:
Question 1: Why are FC's profit margins not as good as those of the new competitor entrant? How do you propose FC fix this problem?

Question 2: Given the issues and recommendations from Question 1, how can FC cut costs, and what are the new expected profit margins?

clarifying_info.q: What are FC's raw material costs relative to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Raw material costs (porcelain clay) are in-line with or less than those of competitors.
Manufacturing takes place at FC's North Carolina headquarters and is efficient; costs are slightly lower than those of competitors.

clarifying_info.q: What does FC's distribution network look like?
clarifying_info.a: FC has 6 warehouses: 2 in North Carolina, 2 in Ohio, and 2 in Southern California. China is manufactured in North Carolina, then distributed to regional warehouses for quicker shipping to retailers when orders are placed.

clarifying_info.q: Where and how does FC sell its china?
clarifying_info.a: The china is sold only as sets through upscale retail stores like Neiman Marcus and Saks Fifth Avenue. Retailers hold only one display set; they do not hold inventory. When a customer orders, the retailer contacts FC for next-day delivery to the store or occasionally a personal home delivery.

clarifying_info.q: What type of shipping service does FC use?
clarifying_info.a: Delivery requires 'white glove service' — no damage or sloppiness permitted. When the company started, they used railroads; in the last 30 years they moved to trucks to transport china from the manufacturing plant to the warehouses.

clarifying_info.q: What does the key competitor's distribution look like?
clarifying_info.a: The key competitor is located in Tennessee (Memphis). They have one warehouse and use FedEx from their manufacturing site to ship quickly to retailers, also with a one-day delivery commitment.

clarifying_info.q: How expensive is common-carrier white glove service compared to FC's current per-box shipping?
clarifying_info.a: Common carrier white glove service costs $150 per set, which is more expensive than FC's current per-box shipping cost allocation.

clarifying_info.q: What is a good proxy for evaluating the fixed cost mix between factory and warehouses?
clarifying_info.a: A good proxy is square footage. The factory is twice the size of the average warehouse.
Pricing is in-line with or slightly higher than competitors. FC's price will not change.

exhibits.title: Fine China, Ltd — Income Statement (Interviewer Only)
exhibits.shows: A two-column income statement showing current costs broken down by category as a percentage of total costs, and a new income statement derived after cost reductions. The exhibit is for the interviewer's use; the candidate must derive figures interactively.
exhibits.data: Revenue: 10,000 sets x $1,500 = $15,000,000; Total Costs (given): $12,000,000; Cost breakdown — Raw Materials 20%, Fixed Overhead 40%, Labor 20%, Shipping 10%, Inventory Costs 10%; Current Profit Margin: 20%

framework: Frame as a profitability AND supply chain case, not purely a cost/revenue issue
Map the value chain: raw materials → manufacturing → distribution → retail → customer
Benchmark each value chain link against the competitor to isolate where the margin gap originates
Identify that raw materials and manufacturing are competitive; focus investigation on distribution
Diagnose the distribution model: 6 warehouses vs. competitor's single warehouse + FedEx
Recommend eliminating most warehouse space and switching to overnight courier (FedEx/UPS)
Quantify the cost impact: warehouse-related fixed overhead, labor, and inventory costs fall; shipping costs rise; net margin improvement is substantial

questions.prompt: Question 1 — Why are FC's margins lower than the competitor's, and how should FC fix this?
questions.guidance: A strong answer recognizes this is a supply chain case disguised as a profitability case. The candidate should walk through the value chain, confirm raw materials and manufacturing are not the issue, then identify the bloated 6-warehouse distribution network as the root cause. The competitor achieves next-day delivery with one warehouse and FedEx — FC replicates that with 6 warehouses and trucks at far higher fixed cost. Recommendation: close most warehouses and shift to overnight carrier (FedEx/UPS) white glove delivery direct from NC manufacturing site.

questions.prompt: Question 2a — Derive the current income statement. What are current profits and profit margin?
questions.guidance: The interviewer tells the candidate that total costs are $12mm. The candidate should name major cost categories; as each is named, the interviewer reveals its share. A strong answer names: Raw Materials, Fixed Overhead (warehouses), Labor, Shipping, Inventory Costs. Once all five are identified, calculate profit margin.

math.setup: Revenue = 10,000 sets x $1,500/set. Total Costs given = $12,000,000. Profit = Revenue - Costs. Margin = Profit / Revenue.

questions.prompt: Question 2b — After closing most warehouses and shifting to FedEx, what are the new expected profit margins?
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify which cost lines change and give intuition for why: Fixed Overhead falls because warehouses are eliminated (keep some space in NC); Labor falls because fewer workers are needed to load and unload at warehouses; Inventory Costs fall because less inventory is held in warehouses; Shipping rises because FedEx white glove is more expensive per set than trucking. Raw Materials are unchanged because production volume stays the same.

math.setup: Apply the percentage changes to each cost line from the current income statement. New Total Costs = sum of revised line items. New Margin = (Revenue - New Total Costs) / Revenue.

recommendation: FC should eliminate most of its regional warehouses (retaining minimal space in North Carolina near the manufacturing plant) and transition from truck-based distribution to overnight courier service (FedEx or UPS) with white glove delivery direct from NC to retail stores
This mirrors the competitor's proven model and increases the profit margin from 20% to approximately 42%, a more than doubling of profitability
risks: Transition risk: logistics disruption during the changeover from trucks/warehouses to FedEx could result in missed deliveries and damage to relationships with luxury retailers
Dependency on a single carrier: reliance on FedEx introduces vulnerability to carrier price increases, service failures, or capacity constraints
Incremental shipping cost is higher per set ($150 for white glove carrier vs. current truck allocation), so if volume ever increases significantly, shipping cost could become a larger burden
Breakage risk: china is fragile; white glove courier handling must be rigorously specified and monitored to protect brand reputation
next_steps: Negotiate white glove service contract with FedEx/UPS and pilot the model with one region before full rollout
Develop a warehouse closure plan and timeline, including lease exits and workforce transition
Establish carrier performance SLAs and breakage/damage tracking metrics
Monitor profit margins quarterly to confirm the 42% target is achieved post-transition
